terms.definition: A number a + bi built from two real numbers and the unit i, where i² = −1; 3 + 4i is one. It can be drawn as a point in a plane, and every amplitude is one.
The length of a complex number z = a + bi, written |z| and equal to √(a² + b²). For 3 + 4i it is 5. Squaring it turns an amplitude into a probability.
The number z = r·e^{iφ}: the same complex number given by its length r and its angle φ from the positive real axis. Multiplying two numbers in this form multiplies the lengths and adds the angles.
A factor e^{iγ} in front of a whole state, as in e^{iγ}|ψ⟩. Every probability stays the same, so |ψ⟩ and e^{iγ}|ψ⟩ are the same physical state.
The angle φ between the two amplitudes of a superposition, as in (|0⟩ + e^{iφ}|1⟩)/√2. A 0/1 measurement cannot see it, but a Hadamard gate turns it into a difference in probabilities.

A system with two distinguishable states |0⟩ and |1⟩ whose state can be any unit vector α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ with complex α and β. A real device builds one from, for example, a superconducting circuit or a trapped ion.
The states |0⟩ and |1⟩ for one qubit, and for n qubits the 2ⁿ states |00…0⟩ to |11…1⟩, one for each bit string. Measuring in this basis returns a bit string.
The complex number in front of a basis state in a superposition. In (|0⟩ + i|1⟩)/√2 the amplitudes are 1/√2 and i/√2, and the probability of an outcome is the squared modulus of its amplitude.
The matrix H = (1/√2)[[1, 1], [1, −1]]. It sends |0⟩ to |+⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2 and |1⟩ to |−⟩ = (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2, and applying it twice gives back the starting state.
Reading a qubit in a chosen basis. It returns one classical outcome, with probability equal to the squared modulus of that outcome's amplitude, and leaves the state in the matching basis state.

⟨u|v⟩ = u₁*v₁ + u₂*v₂ + …, the conjugated entries of u times the entries of v, added up. It is 1 for the same unit vector and 0 for orthogonal ones, and |⟨u|v⟩|² is the probability of finding u when the state is v.
Scaling a state so that |α|² + |β|² + … = 1, which is what makes the probabilities add up to 1. To normalize a vector, divide it by its norm √⟨v|v⟩.

Describes two vectors whose inner product is 0, such as |0⟩ and |1⟩ or |+⟩ and |−⟩. A measurement can tell orthogonal states apart perfectly. A set of orthogonal vectors that all have length 1 is called orthonormal.
The list of complex amplitudes, one per basis state, that fixes a pure state: (1/√2, 1/√2) is |+⟩. For n qubits it has 2ⁿ entries.
A matrix U with U†U = I, so it keeps the length of every state equal to 1. Every gate is unitary, which also makes it reversible: U† undoes U.
The matrix A† you get by flipping A over its diagonal and replacing each entry by its complex conjugate. For a column |v⟩ it gives the row ⟨v|.

A matrix equal to its own conjugate transpose, A = A†, such as X, Y, Z or H. Its eigenvalues are real numbers, so observables and Hamiltonians, whose eigenvalues are measurement results, are Hermitian.
The three 2×2 matrices X = [[0, 1], [1, 0]], Y = [[0, −i], [i, 0]] and Z = diag(1, −1). Together with I they span every 2×2 matrix, and each one squares to I.
A number λ for which some nonzero vector |v⟩, the eigenvector, satisfies A|v⟩ = λ|v⟩: the matrix only rescales it. X has eigenvalue +1 on |+⟩, and an eigenvalue of a unitary is always a phase e^{iφ}.
The average result of measuring an observable O on |ψ⟩, equal to ⟨ψ|O|ψ⟩. For Z on |+⟩ it is 0. In practice you estimate it by averaging many shots.
A Hermitian matrix that stands for something you can measure, like Z. Its eigenvalues are the possible results, and ⟨ψ|O|ψ⟩ is their average on |ψ⟩.
The operation ⊗ that joins two systems: |0⟩ ⊗ |1⟩ = |01⟩. Two qubits have 4 amplitudes and n qubits have 2ⁿ. For matrices, A ⊗ B acts on the two parts independently.
A multi-qubit state that factors into one state per qubit, like |+⟩|0⟩. When no such factoring exists, as for (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, the state is entangled.
A correlation between parts of a state that no product of single-qubit states can reproduce. In (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 each qubit alone gives a random bit, yet the two always agree.
A state described by one state vector |ψ⟩, with nothing hidden. Its density operator is |ψ⟩⟨ψ| and its purity is 1. A state that cannot be written this way is mixed.

The unit sphere whose points are the pure states of one qubit: |0⟩ at the north pole, |1⟩ at the south, |+⟩ and |−⟩ on the x axis. Global phase is dropped, and a gate acts as a rotation of the sphere.
The gate [[0, 1], [1, 0]] that swaps |0⟩ and |1⟩, the quantum NOT. On the Bloch sphere it is a half turn about the x axis.
R_x(θ), R_y(θ) and R_z(θ): the gates that turn the Bloch vector by the angle θ about the x, y or z axis. For example, R_y(π/2) takes |0⟩ to |+⟩.
A state with more than one nonzero amplitude, such as (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2. When measured it gives a single outcome, chosen with probabilities set by the squared amplitudes.
What a measurement does to the state: afterwards it is the basis state that was found, so measuring again gives the same result. Which state it is, is random.
S = diag(1, i). It leaves |0⟩ alone and multiplies |1⟩ by i, a quarter turn about the z axis of the Bloch sphere. Applying S twice gives Z.
What happens when two routes to the same outcome have amplitudes that add or cancel, depending on their relative phase. H followed by H returns |0⟩ because the two routes to |1⟩ cancel.
The four entangled two-qubit states (|00⟩ ± |11⟩)/√2 and (|01⟩ ± |10⟩)/√2, called |Φ±⟩ and |Ψ±⟩. They are orthogonal to each other and together form a basis of two qubits.

A two-qubit gate that flips the target qubit when the control is |1⟩ and does nothing otherwise, so |10⟩ becomes |11⟩. H on the control followed by CNOT turns |00⟩ into the Bell state (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2.
Controlled-U: apply U to the target qubit if the control is |1⟩ and leave it alone if the control is |0⟩. With the control in a superposition, both cases happen together.
A protocol that moves an unknown qubit state from Alice to Bob using a shared Bell pair and two classical bits. Alice's measurement destroys her copy, so nothing is cloned.
No quantum operation takes an unknown |ψ⟩ and a blank |0⟩ to |ψ⟩|ψ⟩ for every |ψ⟩. A CNOT copies |0⟩ and |1⟩, but on |+⟩ it produces a Bell state instead.
The state I/d that tells you nothing: every basis outcome is equally likely. For one qubit it is I/2, the center of the Bloch sphere.
What one part of a larger system looks like on its own, found by ignoring the rest. Each qubit of a Bell pair, taken alone, is maximally mixed.

A state that is a probabilistic mixture, like |0⟩ half of the time and |1⟩ the other half, or one qubit of an entangled pair. No single state vector describes it, and its Bloch vector is shorter than 1.
Exchanges the states of two qubits, and equals three CNOTs. The transpiler inserts it to bring distant qubits next to each other.
The qubit that decides whether a controlled gate acts. In a CNOT the target is flipped only when the control is |1⟩.
How close two states are. For pure states it is |⟨a|b⟩|², which is 1 when they match and 0 when they are orthogonal; for a state ρ and a pure target |a⟩ it is ⟨a|ρ|a⟩.
Encodes a|0⟩ + b|1⟩ as a|000⟩ + b|111⟩. The parity checks Z₀Z₁ and Z₁Z₂ point to a single flipped qubit, and an X on it restores the state.
An extra qubit used as scratch space or to read a parity check, such as the qubits that hold a syndrome. It usually starts in |0⟩.
Sending two classical bits with one qubit, when sender and receiver already share a Bell pair. The sender applies I, X, Z or XZ to her half, and the receiver measures both qubits in the Bell basis.

A game in which Alice and Bob each receive a bit and answer so that the XOR of their answers equals the AND of the bits, without talking. Classical players win at most 75% of the time; with a shared Bell pair they win cos²(π/8) ≈ 85.4%.
The limit |S| ≤ 2√2 on the CHSH quantity for any quantum strategy, against 2 for classical ones. It corresponds to the best quantum winning probability, cos²(π/8) ≈ 85.4%.
Two qubits that never met become entangled when a third party measures one qubit from each of two Bell pairs in the Bell basis. It is teleportation applied to half of an entangled pair.
For a pure two-qubit state α|00⟩ + β|01⟩ + γ|10⟩ + δ|11⟩, the number C = 2|αδ − βγ|. It is 0 for product states and 1 for Bell states.
A state |ψ⟩ that an operator only multiplies by a number, A|ψ⟩ = λ|ψ⟩. |−⟩ is an eigenstate of X with eigenvalue −1, so measuring X on it gives −1 every time.
A black box that evaluates a function, given as a gate U_f taking |x⟩|y⟩ to |x⟩|y ⊕ f(x)⟩. The algorithm sees only what the box returns and is scored by how often it calls it.
When a controlled-U acts on a target that is an eigenstate of U with eigenvalue e^{iφ}, the target stays the same and the control picks up the phase: α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ becomes α|0⟩ + e^{iφ}β|1⟩.
Decides with one oracle call whether a one-bit function is constant or balanced: the answer is written as a relative phase and a Hadamard gate reads it. A classical method has to evaluate f twice.
Given an eigenstate |u⟩ of U with U|u⟩ = e^{2πiφ}|u⟩, it reads φ to n bits: controlled powers of U write φ as phases on n qubits, and an inverse QFT turns them into the bits.
One call to an oracle. Counting queries is how these lessons compare algorithms: Deutsch's algorithm uses one, a classical method needs two.
A function f(x) that returns the same bit for every input, like f(x) = 0. Deutsch's problem asks to tell it apart from a balanced one.
A function that returns 0 on exactly half of the inputs and 1 on the other half. For one bit, f(x) = x and f(x) = 1 − x are the balanced ones.

The n-bit version, for a function promised to be constant or balanced: one query, then a measurement that gives all zeros for constant and anything else for balanced. A deterministic classical method may need 2ⁿ⁻¹ + 1 queries.
Finds a hidden bit string s from an oracle f(x) = s·x mod 2 with a single query. Classically you need n queries, one per bit of s.
A function satisfies f(x) = f(x ⊕ s) for a hidden string s, and the task is to find s. Simon's algorithm needs about n queries, while any classical method needs exponentially many.

One round of Grover's search: the oracle flips the sign of the marked amplitudes, then the diffusion operator reflects all amplitudes about their mean. Each round rotates the state by a fixed angle toward the marked states.
Finds a marked item among N with about (π/4)√N oracle calls, where a classical search needs about N/2, by repeating the Grover iteration. The speedup is quadratic, not exponential.
D = 2|s⟩⟨s| − I, where |s⟩ is the equal superposition of all strings. It sends each amplitude a to 2·mean − a, an inversion about the mean.
|a⟩⟨b|, a column times a row, which makes a matrix. It sends |ψ⟩ to ⟨b|ψ⟩|a⟩, so |s⟩⟨s| projects onto |s⟩.
The unitary that sends |x⟩ to (1/√N) Σ_y e^{2πixy/N}|y⟩. It turns a periodic pattern of amplitudes into a sharp peak at its frequency, and it needs only about n² gates for n qubits.
The smallest r > 0 with f(x + r) = f(x) for all x. Shor's algorithm finds it for f(x) = aˣ mod N, and Simon's problem has the XOR analogue f(x ⊕ s) = f(x).
Factors N by finding the order r of a random a modulo N with phase estimation, then taking gcd(a^(r/2) ± 1, N). It runs in time polynomial in log N, where no classical method is known to.
Given a and N with no common factor, find the smallest r > 0 with aʳ mod N = 1. For a = 2 and N = 15 it is r = 4. Phase estimation solves it, and Shor's algorithm builds on it.
The Hermitian matrix H that gives the energy of a system. Its eigenvalues are the allowed energies, and the state evolves by the unitary e^{−iHt}.
[A, B] = AB − BA, which is zero exactly when A and B commute. For X and Z it is −2iY, so e^{−i(X+Z)t} is not e^{−iXt}e^{−iZt}.
Approximating e^{−i(A+B)t} by n alternating short steps, (e^{−iAt/n} e^{−iBt/n})ⁿ, each easy to run. The error comes from the commutator [A, B] and shrinks as n grows.
For two qubits, H = J Z⊗Z + h(X⊗I + I⊗X): neighbouring spins coupled along z, plus a field along x. The two parts do not commute, so simulating it needs Trotter steps.

Moving the parameters repeatedly a small step against the gradient of the cost: θ ← θ − η·∇C, where η is the learning rate. In a variational circuit the gradient comes from the parameter-shift rule or from finite differences.
A circuit with free angles, chosen in advance, that a classical optimizer tunes: for example R_y(θ) followed by a CNOT. Its shape decides which states it can reach.
For a gate e^{−iθP/2} with a Pauli P, the exact derivative of an expectation value is [f(θ + π/2) − f(θ − π/2)]/2. It costs two extra circuit runs per parameter and works on hardware.
How many times a circuit is run and measured. An estimate from n shots has a statistical error of about 1/√n, so shots trade time for accuracy.
A loop: a circuit prepares |ψ(θ)⟩ and measures ⟨H⟩, a classical optimizer updates θ, and the cycle repeats. The lowest energy found estimates the ground energy from above.
A variational method for combinatorial problems: start in |+…+⟩ and apply p rounds of a cost layer e^{−iγH_C/2} and a mixer layer, tuning the 2p angles so that measurement gives good bit strings.
The lowest-energy eigenstate of a Hamiltonian, with eigenvalue E₀. For H₂ at 0.74 Å the lesson's exact value is E₀ = −1.1373 Ha.
For any normalized |ψ⟩, ⟨ψ|H|ψ⟩ ≥ E₀, because it is an average of energies that are all at least E₀. So any trial state gives an upper bound on the ground energy.
An energy error of about 1.6 mHa (1 kcal/mol), the precision at which computed reaction energies become useful in chemistry.
The simplest guess for the electrons: each one sits in its own lowest orbital. For H₂ on four qubits it is |1100⟩, and the VQE of lesson 3.2 starts from it.
A recipe that turns the operators of electrons into qubit operators, with one qubit per spin orbital and |1⟩ meaning occupied. It writes a molecular Hamiltonian as a sum of Pauli strings.
A tensor product of I, X, Y and Z, one per qubit, like Z⊗Z⊗I⊗X. A Hamiltonian is written as a weighted sum of them, and each string is measured on its own.
Color the vertices of a graph with two colors to maximize the number of edges whose ends differ. A triangle has best cut 2, since its three edges cannot all be cut.
The value a method finds divided by the best possible value. For Max-Cut, a ratio of 1 means an optimal cut.
A diagonal Hamiltonian whose value on each bit string is that string's cost, so its lowest eigenstate is the best answer. For Max-Cut it is the sum of Z_iZ_j over the edges.
The Hamiltonian X₁ + X₂ + … whose evolution moves amplitude between bit strings that differ in one bit. Without it, the cost layer would only add phases and change no probability.
Encoding the same input x again in several layers, with trainable gates in between: R(x), trainable gates, R(x) again. A single qubit gets a much richer function of x this way.
A circuit that encodes a data point in qubits, applies trainable gates and reads a label from a measurement, say the sign of ⟨Z⟩. Training moves the angles to cut the classification error.
The weights λᵢ in |φ⟩ = Σ λᵢ|aᵢ⟩|bᵢ⟩, a sum of orthogonal product states. One nonzero weight means a product state; a Bell state has two, both equal to 1/√2.

A block of single-qubit rotations on every qubit followed by CNOTs between connected neighbours, repeated. It is chosen because the device runs it well, not because of the problem, and each block enlarges the set of reachable states.
An optimizer that perturbs all angles at once by ±c in a random direction and estimates the gradient from just two evaluations per step. It is cheap and tolerates shot noise, but needs many steps.
An optimizer that uses no gradient: it fits a linear model of the cost to recent evaluations and moves inside a trust region that shrinks over time. It suits small problems with a smooth cost.
A flat landscape: for deep random circuits the variance of each gradient shrinks exponentially with the number of qubits, so an optimizer starting at a random point has no direction to follow.
The ground-state energy of a molecule as the atoms move apart. For H₂ the minimum of the curve sits at the bond length, 0.74 Å.
The matrix ρ, with ρ ≥ 0 and Tr ρ = 1, that holds everything measurable about a state. A pure state has ρ = |ψ⟩⟨ψ|, and a mixture of |ψᵢ⟩ with probabilities pᵢ has ρ = Σ pᵢ|ψᵢ⟩⟨ψᵢ|.
The operation that removes a subsystem from ρ by summing over it, leaving the reduced state of the rest. Tracing out one qubit of a Bell pair gives I/2.
Tr(ρ²): 1 for a pure state, falling to 1/d for the maximally mixed state of dimension d. For one qubit the Bloch vector has length √(2 Tr(ρ²) − 1).
Any physically allowed change ρ → E(ρ) of a possibly noisy state: linear, trace-preserving and completely positive. Unitary gates are channels, and so are bit flips and decay.
Matrices Kₖ with Σ Kₖ†Kₖ = I that write a channel as E(ρ) = Σ Kₖ ρ Kₖ†. A bit flip with probability p has K₀ = √(1−p)·I and K₁ = √p·X.
Applies X with probability p and does nothing with probability 1 − p, so |0⟩ becomes |1⟩ with probability p.
Applies Z with probability p. The populations of |0⟩ and |1⟩ stay, but the off-diagonal terms of ρ shrink by a factor 1 − 2p, so |+⟩ drifts toward a 50/50 mixture of |+⟩ and |−⟩.
With probability p the qubit is replaced by the maximally mixed state I/2; otherwise it is untouched. The Bloch vector shrinks by a factor 1 − p in every direction.
Energy loss: |1⟩ decays to |0⟩ with probability γ, while |0⟩ stays put. It is the usual model of T1 relaxation and pulls the Bloch vector toward |0⟩.
Spreading one qubit's state over several physical qubits so that an error can be found by parity checks and undone, without ever measuring the stored state itself.
The bits that the parity checks return. They say where the error is, for example 10 for a flip of qubit 0 in the bit-flip code, without revealing a or b.
A qubit stored in the joint state of several physical qubits, such as a|000⟩ + b|111⟩. Its error rate can be far below that of the physical qubits that carry it.

The physical error rate p* at which a code's logical failure probability equals that of one bare qubit. Below it the code helps and above it the code hurts; for the three-qubit code it is 1/2. It is not the threshold of fault-tolerant computation.
Building circuits so that one faulty gate causes at most one error in each block of encoded data, which the code can then fix. Otherwise the correcting circuit would add more errors than it removes.
The bit-flip code in the ± basis: a|+++⟩ + b|−−−⟩. A Z error swaps + and −, so the same majority logic corrects a single phase flip.
A Pauli operator S, like ZZI, with S|ψ⟩ = |ψ⟩. A stabilizer code is the set of states fixed by several commuting stabilizers, and measuring them gives the syndrome.
The set of states fixed by every stabilizer, where the encoded qubit lives. An error takes the state out of it, and the syndrome says which way.

Nine physical qubits per logical qubit: three blocks of the phase-flip code, each qubit itself replaced by a bit-flip triple. It corrects any single-qubit error, whether a bit flip, a phase flip or both.
Encoding each qubit of a code with another code, level after level. The Shor code is one such pair, with the bit-flip code inside the phase-flip code.
An operator that acts on the encoded qubit, like XXX on a|000⟩ + b|111⟩. It commutes with every stabilizer, so it changes the stored state without producing a syndrome.
The size of the smallest logical operator, counted in qubits it touches. A code of distance d corrects up to ⌊(d−1)/2⌋ errors, so distance 3 corrects one.
A stabilizer code on a grid wrapped into a torus. Each star is X on the four edges at a vertex and each plaquette is Z on the four edges of a face; an error shows up as a pair of violated checks.
If every operation fails with probability below some threshold, a computation of any length can be made as reliable as you like, at a cost that grows only polynomially with its size.
Rewriting a circuit so that it uses only the gates a device runs and only the qubit pairs it connects, adding SWAPs where needed and simplifying where possible.
The graph whose nodes are physical qubits and whose edges are the pairs that can take a two-qubit gate directly. On a line 0–1–2, a CNOT between 0 and 2 needs help.
The small set of gates a device really executes, such as sx, rz and a two-qubit gate like ECR. Every other gate is rewritten in terms of them.
Qiskit's two ways to run circuits: the Sampler returns measured bit strings, and the Estimator returns expectation values of observables.
Loss of the relative phase of a superposition with no energy exchange: the populations stay and the off-diagonal terms of ρ decay. It is the usual model of T2.
A list of the error channels attached to each gate and measurement of a device, used to simulate noisy runs, for example depolarizing noise after each gate and flips at readout.
The time scale on which an excited qubit decays from |1⟩ to |0⟩: the chance that it is still excited falls as e^{−t/T1}.
The time scale on which a superposition loses its phase, so that the off-diagonal terms of ρ shrink as e^{−t/T2}. It cannot exceed 2·T1, because energy decay destroys phase too.
The chance that a measurement reports 0 for a qubit in |1⟩, or the reverse. These probabilities form an assignment matrix, which can be inverted to undo much of the error.
A matrix whose entry (i, j) is the probability of reading bit string i when the true string was j. Inverting it undoes much of the readout error.

How far a gate on hardware is from the ideal one, usually quoted as an average infidelity. Two-qubit gates are typically much worse than single-qubit gates, so counting them estimates the total error.
Reducing the bias of noisy expectation values by running extra circuits and combining their results classically, without any encoding. It costs more shots and does not repair a single run.
Run the circuit at noise levels 1, 3, 5, for example by folding gates, then fit the expectation values and extrapolate back to noise level 0.
The energy of spins s_i = ±1 as a sum of couplings J_ij s_i s_j over pairs plus fields h_i s_i. Optimization problems are written in this form so that the answer is the state of lowest energy.
The same kind of problem written with bits x_i = 0 or 1: the cost is xᵀQx plus a constant, with Q an upper triangular matrix. It follows from the Ising form by s = 1 − 2x.
The situation where no spin configuration satisfies every coupling at once, as on a triangle with an antiferromagnetic coupling on each edge. The best energy then leaves some couplings unsatisfied.

If a Hamiltonian changes slowly and the gap above the ground state stays open, a system that starts in the ground state stays close to the instantaneous ground state. How slow is slow enough is set by the smallest gap.

Finding the lowest-energy state of an Ising problem by starting in the ground state of a transverse field and slowly trading that field for the problem's energy. In practice it is a heuristic: nothing guarantees the sweep is slow enough.

A classical optimization method that flips random spins, always accepts a lower energy, accepts a higher one with probability e^(−ΔE/kT), and lowers the temperature over time. It crosses energy barriers by thermal fluctuations.
Fitting a problem onto hardware that lacks some of its couplings, by representing a logical qubit with a connected chain of physical qubits.
The size F of the ferromagnetic coupling −F Z Z that holds the qubits of a chain together. Too small and the chain breaks in the ground state; too large and the rescaled problem shrinks.

A term added to the energy that is zero when a constraint holds and positive when it is broken, so that an annealer, which has no rules of its own, avoids violations. Its weight must exceed what a violation could gain in the objective.
